01_Formulas_and_balanced_equations.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Interpret and write word equations, balanced symbol equations with state symbols, and use particle models to show that a chemical reaction conserves every atom present.
Deduce the formula of an ionic compound from the charges of its ions, and write a supplied ionic equation that removes unchanged spectator ions.

prerequisites.statement: Write the correct chemical symbol and formula for common elements, atoms and simple ions (from C02: atoms, ions and formulas).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A balanced equation can only be built from formulas that are already correct; this lesson assumes every individual formula is already known, not guessed.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply a whole formula or an atom count by a small whole-number coefficient.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Balancing an equation means multiplying whole formulas by coefficients, so weak multiplication makes every atom count unreliable.

prerequisites.statement: Recall the charges of common ions, such as Mg2+, Al3+, Cl-, O2- and OH-.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deducing an ionic formula depends on knowing each ion's charge before the charges can be balanced to zero.

diagnostic_items.question: How many hydrogen atoms and how many oxygen atoms are shown by $3\mathrm{H_{2}O}$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: 6 hydrogen atoms ($3\times2$) and 3 oxygen atoms ($3\times1$): the coefficient 3 multiplies the whole water formula.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reads the coefficient as if it were the atom count itself, ignoring the subscript inside the formula.
The learner reads only the formula $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ and ignores the coefficient 3 in front of it.
The learner adds the coefficient to the subscript (3+2 and 3+1) instead of multiplying.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner multiplies a coefficient by every atom inside the formula, which is exactly the skill balancing depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Draw three separate water molecules, count the H and O atoms in each one individually, then add the three totals together.

theory_blocks.title: A formula is a fixed recipe for one particle
theory_blocks.body:
Before any calculation, a chemical formula is simply a count of atoms inside one particle. The **molecular formula** of a compound is the number and type of atoms in one molecule, so $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ means one particle made of 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, no more and no less.

If that count changes, the particle is no longer water: [[red:$\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}$ (hydrogen peroxide) is a genuinely different substance, not 'more concentrated' water]].

A particle model makes this visible: draw the atoms of one particle joined together, and the formula is just a shorthand for that drawing.

Once a formula is fixed, it cannot be edited to make a calculation easier - it can only be copied, several times, if more than one particle of that substance is needed.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a formula off a model or a diagram
theory_blocks.body:
A question will often show a molecule as a model or a diagram instead of naming it, and then ask for its formula. The method is simply to count.

- Count the atoms of each element in **one** molecule.
- Write each element's symbol with that count as a subscript, leaving out a subscript of 1.
- For a compound of carbon, write carbon first, then hydrogen, then the remaining elements, as Cambridge does.

The model below shows one molecule of ethanol. It contains 2 carbon atoms, 6 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, so its molecular formula is $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}$.

[[blue:The counting is always done on a single molecule]]: a picture showing three such molecules would still give the formula $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}$, because a formula describes one particle, not how many particles happen to be drawn.

assets.caption: A ball-and-stick model of one molecule of ethanol: counting gives 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and 1 oxygen atoms, so the molecular formula is $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}$.
assets.purpose: Show the atom-counting route from a model to a molecular formula required by C3.1.3.

theory_blocks.title: Coefficient versus subscript, and conservation of atoms
theory_blocks.body:
A chemical equation has two different kinds of number, and they do two different jobs.

- A **subscript**, written inside a formula (the 2 in $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$), fixes how many atoms of one element sit inside a single particle. It belongs to the identity of the substance and is never changed to balance an equation.
- A **coefficient**, written in front of a formula (the 2 in $2\mathrm{H_{2}O}$), counts how many separate, identical particles are present. It is the only number that may be adjusted when balancing.

A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new particles; it cannot create or destroy a single atom.

This is **conservation of atoms**: the total number of atoms of each element must be exactly the same on the reactant side and the product side of a balanced equation.

Balancing is the process of finding the smallest whole-number coefficients that make this true for every element at once.

assets.caption: Before and after particle counts for $2\mathrm{H_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O}$: every atom present before the reaction is still present after it, only regrouped.
assets.purpose: Make atom conservation visible by counting every atom in a before/after picture rather than only trusting the symbolic equation.

theory_blocks.title: A method for balancing by inspection
theory_blocks.body:
1. Write the correct formula of every reactant and product first, and do not change any of them again.
2. Count the atoms of each element on both sides.
3. Balance one element at a time, usually starting with the element that appears in the fewest formulas, by placing a coefficient in front of a whole formula.
4. Leave any free, uncombined element (such as $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ or $\mathrm{H_{2}}$) until last, since changing its coefficient does not disturb elements already balanced elsewhere.
5. Recount every element once all the coefficients are chosen, to confirm the equation is balanced, then reduce the coefficients to the smallest whole-number ratio if they share a common factor.
6. Add state symbols: $(s)$ solid, $(l)$ liquid, $(g)$ gas, $(aq)$ dissolved in water.

theory_blocks.title: From words to a balanced symbol equation
theory_blocks.body:
A word equation such as 'magnesium + oxygen $\rightarrow$ magnesium oxide' names the substances but carries no information about amounts.

Converting it to a symbol equation adds that missing information in two stages: write the correct formula for each named substance, then balance by inspection.

Only after both stages are complete does the equation show how many particles of each substance actually react.

theory_blocks.title: Deducing ionic formulas and writing ionic equations
theory_blocks.body:
An ionic compound is always electrically neutral overall, even though it is built from charged ions.

To deduce its formula: write the charge of each ion, then choose the smallest whole-number subscripts that make total positive charge equal total negative charge.

A fast method is to cross the size of each charge over as the other ion's subscript (then simplify if both numbers share a common factor): $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ with $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ gives $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$, because $(+2)+2\times(-1)=0$.

The same formula can also be deduced without using charges at all, from a model or a diagram of the lattice: count the ions of each kind in the section shown and write that ratio in its simplest whole-number form.

A section containing 3 $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ions and 6 $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions is in the ratio $1:2$, and so gives $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$ again.

When two solutions react and an insoluble solid forms, some ions take no real part in the reaction: they start and end as separate, dissolved ions. These are **spectator ions**.

An ionic equation shows only the ions and particles that actually change, with spectator ions removed from both sides.

For example, silver nitrate solution reacting with sodium chloride solution is fully written as $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)} + \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$;

since $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$ appear unchanged on both sides, the ionic equation is $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)}$.

Only remove an ion when it is genuinely unchanged on both sides of a specific, supplied equation - never from memory alone.

keywords.definition: A fixed count of atoms within one particle of a substance, shown using chemical symbols and subscripts.
A number written in front of a formula in an equation, counting how many identical particles are present.
A number written inside a formula, fixing how many atoms of one element are in a single particle.
An equation in which the total number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
A label (s), (l), (g) or (aq) showing the physical state of a substance in an equation.
An equation showing only the ions and particles that actually change, with spectator ions removed.
An ion that remains dissolved and unchanged on both sides of a reaction.
The number and type of atoms in one molecule of a compound.

worked_examples.statement: **Balancing a combination reaction.** Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Balance the skeleton equation $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgO}$.
knowns: Formulas Mg, O2 and MgO are already correct and must not be edited
unknowns: The coefficients that balance the equation
reasoning: Oxygen appears as $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ on the left but only once inside $\mathrm{MgO}$ on the right, so the right side needs an even number of oxygen atoms: place a 2 in front of $\mathrm{MgO}$.
That coefficient of 2 now also fixes 2 magnesium atoms on the right, which fixes the magnesium coefficient on the left at 2 as well.
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 2 Mg and 2 O atoms. Right side: 2 Mg and 2 O atoms. Both elements match, so the equation is balanced.

worked_examples.statement: **Balancing an equation with three different formulas on one side.** Sodium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to form sodium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. Balance $\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_{2}O} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$.
knowns: Skeleton equation with four correct formulas
Sodium, carbon and oxygen each appear once on the left
unknowns: The coefficients, especially for HCl and NaCl
reasoning: Sodium: 2 atoms are fixed on the left by $\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}$, so the right side needs 2 $\mathrm{NaCl}$.
Chlorine: 2 $\mathrm{NaCl}$ now needs 2 chlorine atoms on the right, so the left side needs 2 $\mathrm{HCl}$.
Hydrogen: 2 $\mathrm{HCl}$ supplies 2 hydrogen atoms, which exactly matches 1 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, so $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ keeps coefficient 1.
Carbon and oxygen were already balanced at 1 $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ throughout, so no further change is needed there.
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 2 Na, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H, 2 Cl. Right side: 2 Na, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 O (water) + 2 O (carbon dioxide) = 3 O, 1 C. Every element matches.

worked_examples.statement: **Why a subscript cannot be changed to balance an equation.** A learner tries to balance $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$ by rewriting the product as $\mathrm{CO_{3}}$ instead of adjusting coefficients. Explain why this is invalid, and balance the equation correctly.
knowns: Skeleton equation with four correct formulas
$\mathrm{CO_{3}}$ is not the same substance as $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$
unknowns: Correct coefficients, and the reason the subscript edit fails
reasoning: Carbon dioxide is, by definition, the substance $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$; writing $\mathrm{CO_{3}}$ silently invents a different (and non-existent, under these conditions) substance rather than balancing anything.
Balancing must instead use coefficients: iron needs 2 on the right ($2\mathrm{Fe}$) to match $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$.

Oxygen: the left side has 3 (from $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$) plus however many $\mathrm{CO}$ molecules are used; the right side has $2\times$ however many $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ molecules are used.

Trying 3 CO and 3 CO2: left oxygen $=3+3=6$, right oxygen $=3\times2=6$, and carbon matches at 3 on each side.
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 2 Fe, 6 O (3 from Fe2O3 + 3 from CO), 3 C. Right side: 2 Fe, 3 C, 6 O. Balanced using only coefficients, with every formula left untouched.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Editing a subscript changes which substance is being described; it is never a legitimate way to fix an atom count.

worked_examples.statement: **Deducing an ionic formula and an ionic equation.** Aluminium ions, $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$, combine with oxide ions, $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, to form aluminium oxide. Deduce its formula, then write the full balanced equation and the ionic equation for silver nitrate solution reacting with sodium chloride solution to form silver chloride precipitate and sodium nitrate solution.
knowns: Full equation substances: AgNO3(aq), NaCl(aq), AgCl(s), NaNO3(aq)
unknowns: Ionic equation with spectator ions removed
reasoning: Crossing charge sizes as subscripts: $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ contributes subscript 2 (from oxygen's charge) and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ contributes subscript 3 (from aluminium's charge), giving $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$.
Check: $2\times(+3) + 3\times(-2) = 6-6 = 0$, so the formula is neutral.
The full equation is $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)} + \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$, already balanced (1 of each formula on each side).
$\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$ appear dissolved and unchanged on both sides, so they are spectator ions and are removed.
worked_examples.solution:
Aluminium oxide: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$.
Full equation: $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)} + \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$.
Ionic equation: $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The ionic equation keeps only the particles that actually change (dissolved ions becoming a solid). Check it: 1 Ag and 1 Cl on each side, and the total charge $(+1)+(-1)=0$ on the left equals the charge 0 of the neutral solid on the right.

worked_examples.statement: **Deducing an ionic formula from a diagram of the lattice.** The diagram shows a section of the lattice of the compound formed between magnesium and chlorine. Deduce the formula of the compound from the relative numbers of ions shown.
knowns: The section drawn contains 3 $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ions and 6 $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions
A lattice is the same pattern repeated, so any section shows the same ratio of ions
reasoning: Count each kind of ion in the section shown: 3 $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and 6 $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$.
Write that as a ratio and simplify it: $3:6=1:2$.
The formula of an ionic compound gives the simplest whole-number ratio of its ions, so one magnesium goes with two chlorines.
Check the charges agree: $(+2)+2\times(-1)=0$, so the compound is neutral, as it must be.
worked_examples.interpretation: Counting ions in a diagram and crossing over the charges are two routes to the same formula; an exam question may hand you either the picture or the charges, so both must work.

assets.caption: A section of the lattice of magnesium chloride: 3 magnesium ions to 6 chloride ions is the ratio $1:2$, so the formula is $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$.
assets.purpose: Give the diagrammatic route to an ionic formula required by C3.1.6, alongside the charge-crossing route.

guided_exercises.statement: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to form ammonia. Balance the skeleton equation $\mathrm{N_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_{3}}$.
hints: Count the nitrogen atoms first: $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ has 2 N atoms but $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$ has only 1, so nitrogen is not yet balanced. Leave $\mathrm{H_{2}}$, the free element, until last.
If you place a 2 in front of $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$, how many nitrogen and how many hydrogen atoms does that fix on the right?
Once the right side is fixed, choose the left-side coefficients of $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ to match exactly.
guided_exercises.answer: $\mathrm{N_{2}} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_{3}}$. Check: left has 2 N and 6 H; right has 2 N and 6 H.
common_errors: Stopping after balancing nitrogen alone and leaving hydrogen unchecked, which leaves 2 H on the left unmatched against 6 H implied on the right.

guided_exercises.statement: Calcium ions, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, combine with hydroxide ions, $\mathrm{OH^-}$, to form calcium hydroxide. Deduce its formula and check that the charges cancel.
hints: Write the charge of each ion clearly above it before choosing any subscript.
Cross the size of each charge over to become the other ion's subscript, remembering that a subscript of 1 is not written.
Multiply each ion's subscript by its own charge and add the results; a correctly deduced formula must give zero.
common_errors: Writing $\mathrm{Ca_{2}OH}$ by crossing the charges onto the wrong ion, or forgetting to bracket $\mathrm{OH}$ before applying the subscript 2 to the whole ion.

exercises.statement: Methane burns completely in oxygen. Balance $\mathrm{CH_{4}} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$ and add state symbols, given that the reaction happens in the gas phase and water is produced as a liquid once cooled.
hints: Balance carbon and hydrogen first, since each appears in only one product.
Count the oxygen atoms needed by the products before fixing the O2 coefficient.
exercises.full_solution: Carbon: 1 on each side already. Hydrogen: 4 on the left needs 2 H2O on the right. Oxygen: the right side then needs $2+2=4$ oxygen atoms, which needs 2 O2 on the left. Check: left 1 C, 4 H, 4 O; right 1 C, 4 H, 4 O.
common_errors: Leaving the O2 coefficient at 1, which supplies only 2 oxygen atoms when the products need 4.

exercises.statement: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas. Balance $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$.
hints: Chlorine appears twice in MgCl2 but only once in HCl.
Fix the HCl coefficient from chlorine, then check hydrogen is already consistent.
exercises.full_solution: Chlorine: MgCl2 needs 2 Cl, so 2 HCl is needed on the left. That also supplies 2 H atoms on the left, matching 1 H2 (which has 2 H atoms) on the right. Magnesium is already 1:1.
common_errors: Leaving HCl at coefficient 1, which balances magnesium but leaves chlorine and hydrogen both short by one.

exercises.statement: Ammonium ions, $\mathrm{NH_{4}^+}$, combine with sulfate ions, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$, to form ammonium sulfate. Deduce its formula and verify that the total charge is zero.
hints: Treat $\mathrm{NH_{4}^+}$ as one unbreakable unit when assigning its subscript.
Cross the charge sizes as before, bracketing any ion that needs a subscript greater than 1.
exercises.full_solution: Sulfate's charge (2) becomes ammonium's subscript, and ammonium's charge (1) becomes sulfate's subscript (which is not written, since 1 is omitted). Brackets around $\mathrm{NH_{4}}$ are required because the subscript 2 must multiply every atom inside the ammonium ion; without brackets it would apply only to the hydrogen written just before it.
common_errors: Writing $\mathrm{NH_{4}SO_{4}}$ (only one ammonium ion, so the total charge is $(+1)+(-2)=-1$), or writing the 2 without brackets so that it applies only to the hydrogen.

exercises.statement: A technician is told only: "calcium carbonate is heated strongly and decomposes to form calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas." Write and balance the full symbol equation, including state symbols, starting entirely from this word description.
hints: Write the correct formula for each named substance before attempting to balance anything.
Count atoms on each side once the skeleton equation is written; decide whether any coefficient other than 1 is actually needed.
exercises.full_solution: Skeleton equation from the formulas: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$. Counting atoms: left has 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O; right has 1 Ca, 1 C, (1+2=3) O. All three elements already match with every coefficient equal to 1, so no further balancing is needed; only the state symbols had to be added.
common_errors: Assuming a word equation always needs large balancing coefficients, and inserting an unnecessary coefficient that then unbalances an element that was already correct.

exercises.statement: A model of one molecule of ethanoic acid is built from 2 carbon atoms, 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms joined together. Deduce the molecular formula of ethanoic acid.
hints: The molecular formula is the number and type of atoms in one molecule, so it is read straight off the model.
Write carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen, giving each element the count you have been told.
exercises.full_solution: One molecule holds 2 C, 4 H and 2 O atoms, so the molecular formula is $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O_{2}}$. Each subscript is simply the count of that element in one molecule, and the counts are not simplified, because a molecular formula states how many atoms are really there rather than a ratio.
common_errors: Cancelling the counts down to $\mathrm{CH_{2}O}$: that is a ratio, not the number of atoms in one molecule.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Formulas and balanced equations'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Formulas and balanced equations' using precise scientific language.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Iron(III) oxide is reduced by hydrogen. Balance $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + \mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$. (b) A student instead writes $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + \mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{H_{2}O_{3}}$ and argues that it must be acceptable because every atom count now matches. Explain, in terms of what a formula represents, why this is not an acceptable equation.
hints: Balance iron first, then use the 3 oxygen atoms in $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ to fix how many water molecules are formed, and only then balance hydrogen.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}O}$. (b) The atom counts do balance, but the student has changed a subscript inside a formula, so the product written is $\mathrm{H_{2}O_{3}}$ and not water. A subscript is part of the fixed identity of a substance, so the equation no longer describes the reaction that actually happens; only the coefficient in front of a formula may be changed, because it counts particles without altering what each particle is.
exam_questions.full_solution: Iron: $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ fixes 2 Fe atoms on the left, so the right side needs $2\mathrm{Fe}$. Oxygen: the 3 oxygen atoms on the left must all end up in water, so the right side needs $3\mathrm{H_{2}O}$. Hydrogen: $3\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ holds 6 hydrogen atoms, so the left side needs $3\mathrm{H_{2}}$. Check: left 2 Fe, 3 O, 6 H; right 2 Fe, 3 O, 6 H.
mark_scheme: (a) Coefficient 2 in front of $\mathrm{Fe}$, matching the 2 iron atoms in $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ (1 mark).
(a) Coefficients 3 in front of $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ and 3 in front of $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, giving 6 H and 3 O on each side (1 mark).
(b) Identifies that the student has altered a subscript, so the product written is no longer water (1 mark).
(b) States that a subscript fixes the identity of a substance and that only coefficients may be adjusted when balancing (1 mark).
common_errors: Accepting the student's equation because the atom counts tally, without noticing that the substance itself has been changed.

exam_questions.statement: Magnesium ions, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, and nitrate ions, $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$, form magnesium nitrate. (a) Deduce its formula. (b) Magnesium nitrate solution is mixed with sodium carbonate solution, and a precipitate of magnesium carbonate forms, leaving sodium nitrate in solution. Write the full balanced equation with state symbols, then write the ionic equation, naming the spectator ions.
hints: For part (a), treat $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$ as one unbreakable ion when bracketing it.
For part (b), balance formula units first, then decide which ions are unchanged on both sides.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}}$. (b) Full equation: $\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$. Ionic equation: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCO_{3}(s)}$, with $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$ as spectator ions.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Each nitrate ion has a charge of $-1$, so two nitrate ions are needed to cancel the $+2$ charge of one magnesium ion: $(+2)+2\times(-1)=0$. The subscript 2 applies to the whole $\mathrm{NO_{3}}$ group, so it is bracketed: $\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}}$. (b) One formula unit of each reactant gives 1 Mg and 1 $\mathrm{CO_{3}}$ group, matching one $\mathrm{MgCO_{3}}$; then 2 $\mathrm{NaNO_{3}}$ are needed on the right to balance the 2 Na from $\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}$ and the 2 nitrate groups from $\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}}$. $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$ appear dissolved and unchanged on both sides, so they are removed from the ionic equation.
mark_scheme: Correct formula $\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}}$ with brackets around the nitrate group (1 mark).
Full equation balanced, including the coefficient 2 on $\mathrm{NaNO_{3}}$ (1 mark).
Correct state symbols on all four formulas (1 mark).
Correct ionic equation with charges balanced and both spectator ions correctly named (2 marks).
common_errors: Naming $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ or $\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}$ as spectator ions, when they are in fact the ions that actually react to form the precipitate.

challenge_questions.statement: In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide to form aluminium oxide and molten iron: $\mathrm{Al} + \mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}} + \mathrm{Fe}$. Balance this equation, showing how you decided the order in which to balance the elements.
hints: Oxygen appears in only one formula on each side ($\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$), so start there: do the two oxides already contain the same number of oxygen atoms?
Fix the aluminium oxide and iron coefficients from the oxide side first, then adjust the free elements last.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Oxygen is fixed at 3 by $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ on the left and by $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$ on the right (both already contain exactly 3 O with coefficient 1), so those two coefficients stay at 1. Iron: $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ supplies 2 Fe, so the right side needs $2\mathrm{Fe}$. Aluminium: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$ needs 2 Al, so the left side needs $2\mathrm{Al}$. Final check: left 2 Al, 2 Fe, 3 O; right 2 Al, 3 O, 2 Fe.
common_errors: Trying to balance the free elements (Al, Fe) before the compounds that fix oxygen, which forces repeated, unnecessary restarts.

challenge_questions.statement:
Iron reacts with steam to form iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄) and hydrogen gas.
(a) Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction. (2 marks)
(b) State the type of reaction occurring. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the mass of Fe₃O₄ formed when 8.4 g of iron reacts completely. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16) (3 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)
(b) Redox reaction (iron is oxidised, hydrogen in water is reduced).
(c) Moles of Fe = 8.4 ÷ 56 = 0.15 mol. From the equation, 3 mol Fe produces 1 mol Fe₃O₄. Moles of Fe₃O₄ = 0.15 ÷ 3 = 0.05 mol. Mᵣ of Fe₃O₄ = 3(56) + 4(16) = 232. Mass = 0.05 × 232 = 11.6 g.

challenge_questions.statement:
Deduce the formula of aluminium oxide, given that aluminium is in Group III and oxygen is in Group VI. Show your working using ion charges. (3 marks)
Then write a balanced equation for the reaction of aluminium oxide with sulfuric acid. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
Al is in Group III, so it forms Al³⁺ ions. O is in Group VI, so it forms O²⁻ ions. To balance charges: 2 × Al³⁺ = +6 and 3 × O²⁻ = −6. Formula: Al₂O₃.
Al₂O₃(s) + 3H₂SO₄(aq) → Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)

mcq.stem: Which equation is correctly balanced?

options.why_wrong: the left side has 2 H and 2 O, but the right side has only 2 H and 1 O: oxygen is not conserved.
this changes a subscript instead of using a coefficient, turning water into hydrogen peroxide, a different substance, and it still leaves oxygen unbalanced (2 O on the left, 4 O on the right).
the left side has 2 H and 4 O, but the right side has 4 H and 2 O: neither element matches.

mcq.explanation: left side 4 H and 2 O; right side 4 H and 2 O ($2\times2=4$ H and $2\times1=2$ O). Every atom is conserved using only coefficients.

mcq.stem: Aluminium ions are $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and oxide ions are $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$. What is the correct formula of aluminium oxide?

options.why_wrong: the total charge is $(+3)+3\times(-2)=-3$, which is not zero, so this formula is not electrically neutral.
this uses each ion's own charge as its own subscript instead of crossing the charges over; the total charge is $3\times(+3)+2\times(-2)=+5$, which is not zero.
the total charge is $2\times(+3)+2\times(-2)=+2$, which is not zero, so charge has not actually been balanced.

mcq.explanation: crossing the charge sizes gives subscripts 2 and 3, and $2\times(+3)+3\times(-2)=6-6=0$, so the compound is neutral.

mcq.stem: Methane burns completely in oxygen. Which equation correctly represents this reaction?

options.why_wrong: the left side supplies only 2 oxygen atoms, but the right side needs 4 (2 in CO2 and 2 in the water): oxygen is not conserved.
this names carbon and unused oxygen gas as products instead of carbon dioxide, which is chemically the wrong reaction for complete combustion.
carbon monoxide, CO, forms only in incomplete combustion, and oxygen is still unbalanced (4 O on the left, only 3 O on the right).

mcq.explanation: left side has 1 C, 4 H, 4 O; right side has 1 C, 4 H, $2+2=4$ O. Complete combustion of methane produces carbon dioxide and water only.

mcq.stem: In $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)} + \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$, which ions are the spectator ions?

options.why_wrong: these are exactly the ions that react together to form the solid product, so they are not unchanged bystanders.
$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is removed from solution as part of the solid AgCl, so it has changed and is not a spectator.
$\mathrm{Ag^+}$ is removed from solution as part of the solid AgCl, so it has changed and is not a spectator.

mcq.explanation: $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$ remain dissolved, unchanged ions on both sides of the equation, so they are removed to leave the ionic equation $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}+\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}\rightarrow\mathrm{AgCl(s)}$.

mcq.stem: A diagram of part of an ionic lattice shows 6 sodium ions, $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$, and 3 oxide ions, $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$. What is the formula of the compound?

options.why_wrong: this is the ratio $1:1$, but the diagram shows twice as many sodium ions as oxide ions; the charges would not cancel either, since $(+1)+(-2)=-1$.
these are the numbers counted in the section drawn, not the simplest whole-number ratio; $6:3$ simplifies to $2:1$.
this reverses the ratio, giving one sodium ion to two oxide ions, and the total charge would be $(+1)+2\times(-2)=-3$.

mcq.explanation: 6 $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ to 3 $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ is the ratio $2:1$, so the formula is $\mathrm{Na_{2}O}$; the charges confirm it, since $2\times(+1)+(-2)=0$.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a subscript and a coefficient?
flashcards.back: A subscript (inside a formula) fixes the atoms in one particle and is never changed. A coefficient (in front of a formula) counts separate particles and is the only number adjusted when balancing.

flashcards.front: What does conservation of atoms mean for a balanced equation?
flashcards.back: The total number of atoms of each element is exactly the same on the reactant side and the product side.

flashcards.front: Why can't $2\mathrm{H_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\rightarrow2\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}$ balance the reaction correctly?
flashcards.back: Changing the subscript turns water into hydrogen peroxide, a different substance, instead of balancing the original reaction; only coefficients may be changed.

flashcards.front: What do the state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) mean?
flashcards.back: Solid, liquid, gas, and dissolved in water (aqueous), respectively.

flashcards.front: How do you deduce the formula of an ionic compound from its ions' charges?
flashcards.back: Write each ion's charge, then cross the size of each charge over as the other ion's subscript, bracketing any multi-atom ion that needs a subscript greater than 1, and check the total charge is zero.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An equation can be balanced by changing the subscript inside a reactant's formula, for example turning $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ into $\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Changing a small number anywhere in the equation looks, at a glance, like it should have the same balancing effect as changing a coefficient.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner edits a subscript instead of placing a number in front of a formula, and the resulting formula no longer represents the original substance.
misconceptions.correct_model: A formula's subscripts are fixed by what the substance actually is. Only the coefficient in front of a formula may be changed, because it just counts how many of that same particle are present.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what real substance the edited formula now represents; if it is a different substance (hydrogen peroxide instead of water), the edit has silently changed the chemistry, not just the numbers.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The coefficient placed in front of a formula is part of the molecular formula itself, so $2\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ is treated as one unit meaning 'two hydrogens, two oxygens'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both the coefficient and the subscripts are small numbers sitting close together, so a learner who has not separated their roles merges them into one count.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: When asked for the number of atoms in $3\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, the learner reports a total that does not come from multiplying the coefficient by each subscript.
misconceptions.correct_model: The coefficient multiplies the whole formula as a separate, independent particle count; the subscripts describe one single particle of that substance.
misconceptions.remediation: Rewrite $3\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ as three separate copies of $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ side by side, and count atoms in each copy before adding the totals.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Ionic charges can be ignored when writing the formula of a neutral ionic compound, so any subscripts 'look about right' as long as both elements are present.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Covalent formulas such as $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ are usually just memorised, so a learner may expect ionic formulas to work the same way, without checking that charge actually cancels to zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes an ionic formula whose total positive and negative charge does not add to zero, often by using each ion's own charge as its own subscript (for example $\mathrm{Al_{3}O_{2}}$ instead of $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$).
misconceptions.correct_model: Every ionic compound is electrically neutral. The subscripts in its formula are chosen so that total positive charge exactly cancels total negative charge.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the charge of each ion above it, then find the smallest whole-number subscripts that make the total charge add to zero, checking by substitution afterwards.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing a subscript inside a formula to try to balance an equation.
common_mistakes.why: This silently changes which substance is being described.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Only ever change the coefficient written in front of a whole formula.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a coefficient and a subscript as one combined number.
common_mistakes.why: Both are small numbers placed close together in the printed equation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Multiply the coefficient by every subscript inside the formula separately, rather than reading them as one quantity.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing an ionic formula without checking that the total charge is zero.
common_mistakes.why: Covalent formulas are often memorised without reference to charge, and that habit carries over incorrectly.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: After crossing the charges, always multiply each subscript by its ion's charge and add the results to confirm they cancel to zero.

common_mistakes.mistake: Removing an ion from an equation as a 'spectator' without checking it is actually unchanged in that specific equation.
common_mistakes.why: Spectator-ion removal can be over-applied as a fixed rule rather than checked case by case.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Only remove an ion once you have confirmed it appears, in the same form, on both sides of that supplied equation.

exam_notes: When asked to balance an equation, write every coefficient explicitly, including a 1 if that helps you check your working, then state the final equation with 1s omitted.
A question asking you to 'explain' an invalid balancing method expects you to say what a subscript represents, not just that the method 'doesn't work'.
For ionic formulas, show the charge-crossing step, not only the final formula, since method marks are usually awarded for it.
When identifying spectator ions, check both sides of the specific equation given rather than relying on which ions you expect to be spectators from memory.

summary.big_idea: A formula fixes the atoms in one particle; a balanced equation uses coefficients, never subscripts, to show that every atom present before a reaction is still present after it.
key_points: Subscripts belong to a formula's identity and are never edited; coefficients count particles and are the only adjustable number.
Balance one element at a time, leaving free elements until last, then confirm every element matches before reducing coefficients.
A word equation becomes a symbol equation in two separate steps: correct formulas first, then balancing.
An ionic compound's formula is chosen so total positive and negative charge cancels to zero.
An ionic equation removes spectator ions that are genuinely unchanged on both sides of a specific equation.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: If you ever change a subscript to balance an equation, you have described a different substance, not balanced the original one.

02_Relative_masses_and_direct_proportion.title: Relative masses and direct proportions
02_Relative_masses_and_direct_proportion.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe relative atomic mass (Ar) as an average compared with carbon-12, and calculate relative formula mass (Mr) by summing the Ar values in a formula.
Calculate a reacting mass from a balanced equation using proportional reasoning based on relative formula masses, without using mole terminology.

theory_blocks.title: Ar is a comparison, not a mass
theory_blocks.body:
Individual atoms are far too light to weigh directly, so chemists instead compare them with one another.

**Relative atomic mass, Ar,** is the average mass of the isotopes of an element compared with $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of an atom of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$: it states how many times heavier the average atom of an element is than $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

Carbon-12 itself is defined to have Ar exactly 12, and every other element's Ar is read from this same scale: hydrogen (Ar = 1) is roughly $\tfrac{1}{12}$ as heavy as carbon-12, oxygen (Ar = 16) is roughly $\tfrac{16}{12}$ as heavy.

Because Ar is the ratio of two masses, the units of mass cancel completely: Ar has [[blue:**no unit**]]. It is a pure comparison, and it stays the same number whether you are thinking about one atom or an enormous collection of them.

theory_blocks.title: Relative formula mass, Mr
theory_blocks.body:
**Relative formula mass, Mr,** is the sum of the Ar values of every atom shown in a formula, counting repeated atoms as many times as the subscript shows. For carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$:
$$M_r(\mathrm{CO_{2}}) = A_r(\mathrm{C}) + 2\times A_r(\mathrm{O}) = 12 + 2\times16 = 44.$$
For a substance made of molecules, such as $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$, this sum is called the **relative molecular mass**; for an ionic compound, such as NaCl, which is not made of molecules, it is called the **relative formula mass**.

Both use the symbol Mr and are calculated in exactly the same way.

Like Ar, Mr has no unit, for the same reason: it is still a ratio compared with $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of a carbon-12 atom, just applied to a whole particle instead of a single atom.

theory_blocks.title: From a balanced equation to a reacting-mass ratio
theory_blocks.body:
A balanced equation already fixes the ratio in which particles react. To turn that into a **mass** ratio, multiply each substance's coefficient by its own Mr; do not use the bare coefficients:
$$\text{mass ratio term for a substance} = (\text{its coefficient}) \times (\text{its } M_r).$$
For $2\mathrm{H_{2}} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, with $A_r(\mathrm{H})=1$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$: $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$, $M_r(\mathrm{O_{2}})=32$, $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}O})=18$, so the mass ratio is $2\times2: 1\times32: 2\times18 = 4:32:36$.

Once this stoichiometric ratio is known, any single reacting mass can be scaled up or down proportionally: if 8 g of $\mathrm{H_{2}}$ reacts completely, the scale factor is $8\div4=2$, so $32\mathrm{\ g}$ of $\mathrm{O_{2}}$ is needed and $36\times2=72\mathrm{\ g}$ of $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ is made.

Always check: $8+64=72$, so mass is conserved.

assets.caption: Reacting-mass ratio for $2\mathrm{H_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\rightarrow2\mathrm{H_{2}O}$: bar height is each side's (coefficient $\times$ $M_r$), so $4+32=36$ shows mass is conserved.
assets.purpose: Show the mass ratio 4:32:36 as directly comparable bar heights, making visible that it is built from coefficient times Mr, not from the coefficients alone.

theory_blocks.title: A preview, not yet the full story
Why Ar is usually not a whole number: averaging isotopes
theory_blocks.body:
**Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** 0654 asks you only to *describe* $A_r$ as the average mass of the isotopes of an element compared with $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of an atom of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$; working that average out from isotope abundances is not examined in this course. It is kept here because it explains where a value such as 35.5 comes from.

Most elements exist naturally as a mixture of isotopes: atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so slightly different masses.

The Ar printed on a periodic table is the **abundance-weighted average** across all of an element's naturally occurring isotopes, not the mass number of any single isotope.

For chlorine, about 75% of atoms are $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and about 25% are $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$:
$$A_r(\mathrm{Cl}) = 0.75\times35 + 0.25\times37 = 35.5.$$
Notice that 35.5 is not the mass number of either isotope on its own; it only appears once both isotopes are weighted by how common each one actually is.

keywords.definition: How many times heavier the average atom of an element is than 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom; no unit.
The sum of the Ar values of every atom shown in a formula; no unit.
An atom of an element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons, and so a different mass.
The percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope.
The ratio (coefficient × Mr) for each substance in a balanced equation.
The number obtained by dividing an actual mass by its stoichiometric mass, used to scale every substance in a reaction proportionally.

worked_examples.statement: **Relative formula mass of carbon dioxide.** Calculate $M_r(\mathrm{CO_{2}})$, given $A_r(\mathrm{C})=12$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$.
reasoning: Add one Ar(C) and two Ar(O), since the subscript 2 shows two oxygen atoms in every CO2 particle.
worked_examples.interpretation: The answer has no unit: it is a comparison with $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of a carbon-12 atom, applied to the whole CO2 particle.

worked_examples.statement: **Relative formula mass with three different elements.** Calculate $M_r(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}})$, given $A_r(\mathrm{Ca})=40$, $A_r(\mathrm{C})=12$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$.
reasoning: Every element's subscript must be counted separately before adding: here the 3 applies only to oxygen.
worked_examples.interpretation: A useful round number: calculations involving calcium carbonate (for example, how much carbon dioxide it gives off when heated) become especially easy to scale.

worked_examples.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** **Why Ar is not the most abundant isotope's mass number.** Chlorine occurs as 75% $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and 25% $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$. Explain why $A_r(\mathrm{Cl})\neq35$ and calculate its actual value.
reasoning: $A_r$ is defined as the average mass across every atom actually present, so the rarer, heavier isotope must still pull the average upward from 35.
Weight each isotope's mass number by its fraction of all atoms, then add the two weighted values.
worked_examples.interpretation: 35.5 sits between the two mass numbers, closer to 35 because that isotope is more common; it equals neither isotope's own mass number, confirming that 'most abundant isotope' thinking gives the wrong value (35, not 35.5).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting Ar as simply 35, the mass number of the more common isotope, instead of the abundance-weighted average of both isotopes.

worked_examples.statement: **Reacting mass from a balanced equation.** Magnesium burns in oxygen: $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$. Given $A_r(\mathrm{Mg})=24$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$, calculate the mass of oxygen needed, and the mass of magnesium oxide formed, when 12 g of magnesium reacts completely.
reasoning: Build the stoichiometric mass ratio first: $M_r(\mathrm{Mg})=24$ so $2\mathrm{Mg}$ has mass $48$; $M_r(\mathrm{O_{2}})=32$; $M_r(\mathrm{MgO})=40$ so $2\mathrm{MgO}$ has mass $80$. The ratio is $48:32:80$, which already checks as $48+32=80$.
The actual mass of Mg (12 g) fixes a scale factor relative to the stoichiometric 48 g: this scale factor applies equally to every substance in the equation.
worked_examples.solution: Scale factor $= 12\div48 = 0.25$. Mass of $\mathrm{O_{2}} = 0.25\times32 = 8\mathrm{\ g}$. Mass of $\mathrm{MgO} = 0.25\times80 = 20\mathrm{\ g}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $12+8=20$, so mass is conserved, confirming the scale factor was applied consistently to every substance.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the bare coefficient ratio 2:1:2 directly on 12 g, instead of first weighting each coefficient by its Mr.

hints: List the Ar value for each of the three different elements in the formula.
Every element here has subscript 1, so each Ar is added exactly once.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the hydrogen atom and calculating only $23+16=39$.

guided_exercises.statement: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$, with $M_r(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}})=100$, $M_r(\mathrm{CaO})=56$ and $M_r(\mathrm{CO_{2}})=44$. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide and the mass of carbon dioxide formed when 50 g of calcium carbonate decomposes completely.
hints: Confirm the stoichiometric mass ratio $100:56:44$ checks as $56+44=100$ before scaling anything.
Find the scale factor by dividing the actual CaCO3 mass by its stoichiometric mass, 100.
Apply the same scale factor to both CaO and CO2.
guided_exercises.answer: Scale factor $=50\div100=0.5$. Mass of $\mathrm{CaO}=0.5\times56=28\mathrm{\ g}$. Mass of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}=0.5\times44=22\mathrm{\ g}$.
common_errors: Forgetting to scale the mass ratio at all, and simply reporting the stoichiometric masses 56 g and 44 g regardless of the 50 g actually used.

exercises.statement: Calculate $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}})$, given $A_r(\mathrm{H})=1$, $A_r(\mathrm{S})=32$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$.
hints: There are 2 hydrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms in this formula.
exercises.full_solution: Each subscript is applied to its own element only: 2 for hydrogen, 1 (unwritten) for sulfur, 4 for oxygen.
common_errors: Multiplying the whole formula's total by a single subscript instead of applying each subscript to its own element.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** Boron occurs as 20% $^{10}\mathrm{B}$ and 80% $^{11}\mathrm{B}$. Calculate $A_r(\mathrm{B})$ and explain why your answer is closer to 11 than to 10.
hints: Weight each isotope's mass number by the fraction of atoms with that mass number.
The isotope that is more abundant should pull the average closer to its own mass number.
exercises.full_solution: Because 80% of boron atoms are the heavier isotope ($^{11}\mathrm{B}$), the weighted average sits much closer to 11 than to 10.
common_errors: Taking a simple average of 10 and 11 (giving 10.5) instead of weighting by the actual percentages.

exercises.statement: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$, with $M_r(\mathrm{Mg})=24$, $M_r(\mathrm{HCl})=36.5$, $M_r(\mathrm{MgCl_{2}})=95$ and $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$. If 12 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid, calculate the mass of magnesium chloride and the mass of hydrogen produced.
hints: Build the stoichiometric masses first: 1×24, 2×36.5, 1×95, 1×2.
Find the scale factor from the Mg mass, then apply it to MgCl2 and H2 only (HCl is in excess, so it is not needed for this question).
exercises.answer: Scale factor $=12\div24=0.5$. Mass of $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}=0.5\times95=47.5\mathrm{\ g}$. Mass of $\mathrm{H_{2}}=0.5\times2=1.0\mathrm{\ g}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check using the HCl actually consumed: $0.5\times2\times36.5=36.5\mathrm{\ g}$ of HCl reacts, and $12+36.5=48.5\mathrm{\ g}$ in total matches $47.5+1.0=48.5\mathrm{\ g}$ of products.
common_errors: Using the 2:1 coefficient ratio of HCl:H2 as if it applied to Mg:H2, whose coefficients are actually 1:1.

exercises.statement: The Haber process makes ammonia: $\mathrm{N_{2}} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_{3}}$, with $M_r(\mathrm{N_{2}})=28$, $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$ and $M_r(\mathrm{NH_{3}})=17$. A plant reacts 56 kg of nitrogen completely. Using the same proportional method as for magnesium and oxygen, calculate the mass of hydrogen needed and the mass of ammonia produced, in kilograms.
hints: This equation has three different coefficients and three different Mr values, unlike the simpler 1:1 examples seen so far; build the full stoichiometric mass ratio before scaling.
The method transfers exactly: only the numbers and the unit (kg instead of g) are different.
exercises.answer: Scale factor $=56\div28=2$. Mass of $\mathrm{H_{2}}=2\times(3\times2)=12\mathrm{\ kg}$. Mass of $\mathrm{NH_{3}}=2\times(2\times17)=68\mathrm{\ kg}$.
exercises.full_solution: Stoichiometric masses: $\mathrm{N_{2}}=28$, $3\mathrm{H_{2}}=6$, $2\mathrm{NH_{3}}=34$, which checks as $28+6=34$. Scaling by 2 (since 56 kg is twice the stoichiometric 28 kg) gives 12 kg H2 and 68 kg NH3; check $56+12=68$.
common_errors: Using only the H2 formula mass (2) rather than (coefficient × Mr) = 3×2 = 6 as the stoichiometric hydrogen mass before scaling.

exercises.statement: Copper(II) oxide is reduced by hydrogen: $\mathrm{CuO} + \mathrm{H_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$, with $M_r(\mathrm{CuO})=80$, $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$, $M_r(\mathrm{Cu})=64$ and $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}O})=18$. Calculate the mass of copper formed and the mass of hydrogen used when 20 g of copper(II) oxide is reduced completely.
hints: Every coefficient here is 1, so the mass ratio is simply the four $M_r$ values in the order of the equation.
Find the scale factor from the substance whose mass you were given, then apply that same factor to every other substance.
exercises.answer: Mass ratio $80:2:64:18$; scale factor $=20\div80=0.25$. Mass of copper $=0.25\times64=16\mathrm{\ g}$; mass of hydrogen $=0.25\times2=0.5\mathrm{\ g}$.
exercises.full_solution: All four coefficients are 1, so each mass-ratio term is that substance's own $M_r$: $80:2:64:18$. The 20 g of $\mathrm{CuO}$ is a quarter of the stoichiometric 80 g, so every other mass is a quarter of its ratio term: copper $0.25\times64=16\mathrm{\ g}$, hydrogen $0.25\times2=0.5\mathrm{\ g}$, water $0.25\times18=4.5\mathrm{\ g}$. Conservation check: $20+0.5=20.5$ and $16+4.5=20.5$.
common_errors: Scaling only the substance the question asks for, and never checking that the reactant masses and the product masses still add up to the same total.

exercises.statement: Define the key terms used in the study of 'Relative masses and direct proportions'.
exercises.answer: Key definitions should cover the main concepts from 'Relative masses and direct proportions' using precise scientific language.

exam_questions.statement: Ammonium sulfate, $\mathrm{(NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}}$, is a common fertiliser. (a) Calculate its relative formula mass, given $A_r(\mathrm{N})=14$, $A_r(\mathrm{H})=1$, $A_r(\mathrm{S})=32$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$. (b) State the unit of your answer and explain why it has that unit.
hints: Count the atoms inside the brackets, multiply by the bracket's own subscript, then add the part outside the brackets.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $M_r = 132$. (b) No unit: Mr is a ratio compared with $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so the mass units cancel.
exam_questions.full_solution: Inside the brackets: $N + 4H = 14+4=18$ per $\mathrm{NH_{4}}$ unit, times 2 gives 36. Outside the brackets: $S+4O=32+64=96$. Total: $36+96=132$.
mark_scheme: Correctly doubles the $(\mathrm{NH_{4}})$ group before adding (1 mark).
Correct total, 132 (1 mark).
States Mr has no unit (1 mark).
Links this correctly to Mr being a ratio/comparison rather than an actual mass (1 mark).
common_errors: Multiplying only the nitrogen inside the bracket by 2, forgetting that the bracket's subscript 2 multiplies every atom inside it, including all 4 hydrogens.

exam_questions.statement: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$, with $M_r(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}})=100$, $M_r(\mathrm{CaO})=56$ and $M_r(\mathrm{CO_{2}})=44$. A sample of 40 g of calcium carbonate is heated until it decomposes completely. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide formed and the mass of carbon dioxide gas released, and show that your answer is consistent with conservation of mass.
hints: Find the scale factor from the stoichiometric mass of CaCO3, 100.
Apply the same scale factor to CaO and CO2.
exam_questions.answer: Scale factor $=40\div100=0.4$. Mass of $\mathrm{CaO}=0.4\times56=22.4\mathrm{\ g}$. Mass of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}=0.4\times44=17.6\mathrm{\ g}$. Check: $22.4+17.6=40\mathrm{\ g}$, matching the original mass of calcium carbonate.
exam_questions.full_solution: The stoichiometric masses 100, 56 and 44 already satisfy $56+44=100$, so any scale factor applied equally to all three keeps that same conservation relationship true.
mark_scheme: Correct scale factor, 0.4 (1 mark).
Correct mass of CaO, 22.4 g (1 mark).
Correct mass of CO2, 17.6 g (1 mark).
Explicit conservation check: 22.4 + 17.6 = 40 g (1 mark).
common_errors: Calculating one product mass correctly but then finding the other by subtracting from the stoichiometric total (100) instead of from the actual sample mass (40).

challenge_questions.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** Bromine occurs as 51% $^{79}\mathrm{Br}$ and 49% $^{81}\mathrm{Br}$. (a) Calculate $A_r(\mathrm{Br})$, rounding sensibly. (b) Using your rounded value and $A_r(\mathrm{Mg})=24$, calculate $M_r(\mathrm{MgBr_{2}})$.
hints: Weight each isotope's mass number by its percentage, as with chlorine.
A sensible GCSE rounding of a value such as 79.98 is to one decimal place or to the nearest whole number; state which you use.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Unlike chlorine, bromine's two isotopes have almost equal abundance (51% and 49%), so the weighted average (79.98, rounding to 80.0) sits almost exactly halfway between 79 and 81, close to a simple average - but this is a coincidence of similar abundances, not a general rule.
common_errors: Assuming the near-50:50 split means a simple, unweighted average is always valid for isotope abundance calculations, rather than checking the actual percentages each time.

challenge_questions.statement:
A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass.
(a) Calculate the empirical formula. (Aᵣ: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16) (3 marks)
(b) The relative molecular mass is 180. Determine the molecular formula. (2 marks)
(c) Suggest the identity of this compound and one use. (1 mark)
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) C: 40.0/12 = 3.33; H: 6.7/1 = 6.7; O: 53.3/16 = 3.33. Divide by smallest (3.33): C = 1, H = 2, O = 1. Empirical formula: CH₂O.
(b) Empirical formula mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30. Ratio = 180/30 = 6. Molecular formula: C₆H₁₂O₆.
(c) Glucose. Used in respiration by living organisms / as an energy source.

challenge_questions.statement:
Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. (Aᵣ: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16) (2 marks)
Explain why ammonium nitrate is a particularly effective fertiliser, referring to its composition. (2 marks)
challenge_questions.answer:
Mᵣ of NH₄NO₃ = 14 + 4(1) + 14 + 3(16) = 80. Mass of N = 2 × 14 = 28. Percentage N = (28/80) × 100 = 35.0%.
Ammonium nitrate is effective because it contains two nitrogen atoms per formula unit — one in the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) and one in the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻). This gives it a high percentage of nitrogen (35%), which is the nutrient plants need most for growth.

mcq.stem: What is $M_r(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}})$, given $A_r(\mathrm{Ca})=40$, $A_r(\mathrm{C})=12$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O})=16$?

options.why_wrong: this uses only one oxygen atom ($40+12+16$) instead of the three shown by the subscript.
this multiplies oxygen by 2 instead of by the correct subscript, 3 ($40+12+32$).
this doubles the calcium by mistake, as if the formula were $\mathrm{Ca_{2}CO_{3}}$ ($80+12+48$).

mcq.stem: In $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$ ($M_r(\mathrm{Mg})=24$, $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$), what mass of hydrogen is produced when 48 g of magnesium reacts completely?

options.why_wrong: this wrongly applies HCl's coefficient (2) to the Mg:H2 ratio, which is actually 1:1.
this scales using the Mr of HCl (36.5) instead of the Mr of H2 (2).
this assumes mass transfers 1:1 from reactant to product, ignoring both substances' actual Mr values.

mcq.explanation: Scale factor $=48\div24=2$; Mg and H2 have equal coefficients (1 and 1), so mass of H2 $=2\times2=4\mathrm{\ g}$.

mcq.stem: What is the correct unit for a relative formula mass (Mr) value?

options.text: No unit - Mr is a ratio

options.why_wrong: Mr is not yet an actual mass of any sample; it only becomes grams once an amount in moles is specified, in the next lesson.
g/mol is the unit of molar mass, a related but different quantity introduced once the mole is defined.
GCSE relative formula mass is defined as a dimensionless ratio compared with carbon-12, not reported in atomic mass units.

mcq.explanation: Mr compares a formula's mass with $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of one carbon-12 atom; since it is a ratio of two masses, the units cancel.

mcq.stem: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** Chlorine consists of 75% $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and 25% $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$. What is $A_r(\mathrm{Cl})$?

options.why_wrong: this is a simple, unweighted average of 35 and 37, which ignores that the two isotopes are not equally abundant.
this reports only the more abundant isotope's mass number, with no averaging at all.
this reports only the less abundant isotope's mass number, which is not even the closer of the two to the true average.

mcq.stem: Hydrogen reacts with chlorine: $\mathrm{H_{2}} + \mathrm{Cl_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}$, with $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$, $M_r(\mathrm{Cl_{2}})=71$ and $M_r(\mathrm{HCl})=36.5$. What mass of hydrogen chloride is formed when 7.1 g of chlorine reacts completely?

options.why_wrong: this scales only one $\mathrm{HCl}$ formula unit ($0.1\times36.5$); the equation makes two, so the ratio term is $2\times36.5=73$.
this is the stoichiometric ratio term itself, which is the mass of $\mathrm{HCl}$ formed from 71 g of chlorine, not from 7.1 g.
this simply doubles the mass of chlorine; a mass ratio comes from each coefficient multiplied by its own $M_r$, never from doubling a given mass.

mcq.explanation: The mass ratio is $1\times2 : 1\times71 : 2\times36.5 = 2:71:73$. The scale factor is $7.1\div71=0.1$, so the mass of $\mathrm{HCl}$ is $0.1\times73=7.3\mathrm{\ g}$, and $0.2+7.1=7.3$ confirms mass is conserved.

flashcards.front: What does relative atomic mass (Ar) mean?
flashcards.back: How many times heavier the average atom of an element is than 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom; it has no unit.

flashcards.front: How do you calculate Mr from a formula?
flashcards.back: Add the Ar of every atom shown, multiplying each element's Ar by its own subscript first.

flashcards.front: Is the relative atomic mass of an element the mass number of its most common isotope?
flashcards.back: No. Ar is the abundance-weighted average across all naturally occurring isotopes, e.g. Ar(Cl) = 0.75×35 + 0.25×37 = 35.5, not 35.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between using bare coefficients and using a true mass ratio from a balanced equation?
flashcards.back: A mass ratio needs (coefficient × Mr) for each substance; the bare coefficients alone only give a particle ratio, not a mass ratio, unless every Mr happens to be equal.

flashcards.front: If a balanced equation's stoichiometric masses are known, how do you find the mass of product from a different starting mass of reactant?
flashcards.back: Divide the actual reactant mass by its stoichiometric mass to get a scale factor, then multiply every other stoichiometric mass in the equation by that same scale factor.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Relative formula mass, Mr, is measured in grams, so a value such as 'Mr = 44' is treated as meaning '44 g'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Mr is built from masses, and GCSE practical work constantly uses grams, so a learner may attach the most familiar mass unit without checking.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes a unit of grams after an Ar or Mr value, or treats an Mr calculation as already giving a usable laboratory mass.
misconceptions.correct_model: Ar and Mr are ratios compared with 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom, so they have no unit. They only become an actual mass once a real quantity of substance (grams per mole) is specified, which is introduced in the next lesson.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what the number is being compared with; since it is a ratio of two masses, the units cancel and nothing is left to write.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The coefficients in a balanced equation are themselves the reacting-mass ratio, so '2' and '1' directly mean a 2:1 mass ratio.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Coefficients are the first ratio a learner meets in an equation, so it is tempting to use them without the extra step of weighting by formula mass.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner scales reacting masses using the bare coefficients instead of multiplying each coefficient by its formula's Mr first.
misconceptions.correct_model: The reacting-mass ratio is (coefficient $\times$ Mr) for each substance, not the coefficients alone, because different formulas have different masses even when their coefficients are equal.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a reaction where two substances share the same coefficient but different Mr, and show that their mass ratio is not 1:1.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The relative atomic mass of an element is just the mass number of its most abundant isotope.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Most-abundant-isotope thinking is a reasonable first guess, and for several common elements the Ar does sit close to one isotope's mass number, which can look like confirmation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reports an Ar equal to a single isotope's mass number, with no reference to the relative abundance of each isotope.
misconceptions.correct_model: Ar is an abundance-weighted average over every naturally occurring isotope of that element, not the mass number of any one isotope on its own.
misconceptions.remediation: Work through chlorine's two isotopes explicitly: Ar(Cl) = 0.75×35 + 0.25×37 = 35.5, which is neither isotope's mass number.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing a unit of grams after an Ar or Mr value.
common_mistakes.why: Ar and Mr are ratios of two masses (compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom), so the units cancel.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember Ar and Mr are always compared with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom and never carry a unit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Scaling reacting masses using the bare coefficients from a balanced equation.
common_mistakes.why: Coefficients give a particle ratio, not a mass ratio.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always multiply each coefficient by its own Mr before comparing substances by mass.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting an element's Ar as the mass number of its most abundant isotope.
common_mistakes.why: A single isotope's mass number ignores every other isotope actually present.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Weight every isotope's mass number by its percentage abundance and add the weighted values.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that a bracket's subscript multiplies every atom inside the bracket.
common_mistakes.why: It is easy to apply the bracket subscript only to the first element written inside it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate the mass of everything inside one bracket first, then multiply that whole subtotal by the bracket's subscript.

exam_notes: State explicitly that Mr has no unit if a question asks you to justify your answer; this is a common method mark.
Show the stoichiometric mass ratio (coefficient × Mr for each substance) as a separate step before scaling, since method marks are usually awarded for it.

An isotope question in 0654 asks you to *describe* Ar, not to calculate it: learn the sentence "the average mass of the isotopes of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12" and quote it in full.
Always finish a reacting-mass question with an explicit conservation check (reactant mass = sum of product masses) where the question allows it.

summary.big_idea: Ar and Mr are unit-free comparisons with carbon-12; weighting each equation coefficient by its own Mr turns a balanced equation into a reacting-mass ratio that can be scaled to any actual mass, all without using the mole.
key_points: Ar is the abundance-weighted average across all of an element's naturally occurring isotopes, never a single isotope's mass number.
Mr is the sum of Ar values in a formula, applying each subscript (including inside brackets) to its own element only.
Neither Ar nor Mr has a unit, because both are ratios compared with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.
A reacting-mass ratio needs (coefficient × Mr) for each substance, not the bare coefficients alone.
Once a stoichiometric mass ratio is found, any single actual mass sets a scale factor that applies equally to every substance in the equation.
formulas: \text{scale factor} = \dfrac{\text{actual mass of one substance}}{\text{its stoichiometric mass}}
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A mass ratio from an equation always needs coefficient times Mr for every substance - never the coefficients on their own.

epistemic_overrides.note: Ar values from the periodic table are weighted averages of isotopic masses, and GCSE exams use rounded values. This is an exam convention worth marking.

03_The_mole_connects_mass_and_particles..subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: State that one mole of a specified entity (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units) contains 6.02×10²³ of that entity, the Avogadro constant.
Use n = m/M to convert between mass, amount in moles and molar mass, and reverse the relationship to find mass or molar mass.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate Mr from Ar values, and know that Mr has no unit.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Molar mass is numerically equal to Mr, but is given a unit (g/mol); confusing the two quantities carries the an earlier lesson misconception straight into this lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Read and use a number written in scientific notation, such as 6.02×10²³.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every particle-count calculation in this lesson multiplies or divides by a number in scientific notation.
